claim: Averaged across 30 task x model combinations, semantic entropy achieves AUROC 0.790 for hallucination detection, beating naive predictive entropy (0.691), a 'P(True)' self-check baseline (0.698), and an embedding-regression baseline (0.687).
stance_target: sampling/internal-derived uncertainty signals outperforming self-report-style baselines (P(True)) for correctness/hallucination prediction
scope_conditions: TriviaQA, SQuAD 1.1, BioASQ, SVAMP, NQ-Open -- general QA and math, NOT code; whole-answer granularity; LLaMA/Falcon/Mistral 7B-70B
quoted_support: Averaged across 30 task x model combinations, semantic entropy achieves AUROC 0.790, beating naive predictive entropy (0.691), a 'P(True)' self-check baseline (0.698), and an embedding-regression baseline (0.687).

claim: The canonical semantic entropy method has never been validated on code generation, and neither have its cheap single-pass approximations (Semantic Entropy Probes) -- a clean domain gap for a code-LLM confidence/probe paper.
stance_target: novelty of extending internal-signal-vs-verbalization comparisons to the code domain
scope_conditions: Domain gap claim; evaluation datasets are TriviaQA/SQuAD/BioASQ/SVAMP/NQ-Open, none of which are code benchmarks
quoted_support: Evaluation datasets: TriviaQA, SQuAD 1.1, BioASQ (2023 Task B), SVAMP (math word problems), NQ-Open -- general QA and elementary math, NOT code generation.

claim: On a second experiment (GPT-4 paragraph-length biographies, 150 manually labeled factual claims), P(True) briefly edges ahead of discrete semantic entropy once more than 80% of questions are rejected, showing self-report baselines are not uniformly worse across all operating regimes.
stance_target: the claim that internal/sampling signals always strictly dominate self-report baselines
scope_conditions: GPT-4 biography generation, high-rejection-rate operating regime, whole-claim granularity
quoted_support: discrete SE beats self-check and P(True) baselines on both AUROC and AURAC (area under rejection-accuracy curve), with the caveat that P(True) briefly edges ahead once >80% of questions are rejected.
